source.title: Effective Does Not Mean Useful: Conditional Functional Substitutability for Redundancy and Scaling in Transformers
source.authors: Jia-Heng Chen; Jia-Xing Li; Yu-Cheng Xiao; Xin-Yong Cai; Jun-Cheng Bu; Lan-Ting Yu; Ting-He Zhang

record.file_problem: The text is the full paper. Some figure text is garbled, but the relevant fixed-capacity results are readable in Table 5 and the main text.
record.tranche_reason: It tests whether architectural decomposition changes language-model validation loss at fixed parameter count, using a head-granularity comparison rather than a scaling-law fit.
record.gate_note: The study does not fit or test power laws, extrapolation from small runs, compute-optimal allocations, or downstream predictability. Its fixed-capacity head-decomposition comparison does test V4. Other scaling results focus on functional organization and do not establish the power-law or compute-optimal claims.
record.test_reason: Section 5.3 / Table 5 trains three GPT-2-style models from scratch at identical 124.44M parameters (12 layers, width 768) that differ only in head decomposition. It reports validation loss, which bears directly on V4 at fixed parameter count. No other result fits or tests power laws (V1, V2, V5), compute-optimal allocation (V3), downstream prediction (V6) or fitting choices (V7).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors report that at fixed capacity the head decomposition with lower substitutability and higher normalized functional rank (6×128) has the lowest validation loss. They call this associative, not causal, because head granularity also changes inductive bias, and they conclude that parameter count alone does not determine functional organization. They do not comment on whether the loss differences are practically small. Their wider claim is that CFS gives a microscopic functional account of diminishing returns in scaling.
record.recipe_differences: The study measures validation loss across head decompositions at fixed capacity; it does not use the original scaling-law fitting or compute-optimal allocation method.
record.method_sensitivity: Head granularity changes the measured validation loss and functional-organization metrics at fixed parameter count.

fits_no_version.finding: From a shared 124.44M baseline, deepening to 18 layers (166.97M, loss 3.5024) gives a larger loss reduction per added parameter than widening to width 1152 (250.36M, loss 3.4000). Parameter counts are not matched, so this is not a fixed-parameter shape test. The authors say it should not be read as depth being generally preferable.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Parameter efficiency of scaling differs between depth and width growth paths at small GPT-2 scale.

record.code_released: Code, evaluation scripts, and configurations will be released upon acceptance.
record.problems: The fixed-capacity comparison covers only three head decompositions and reports no uncertainty estimates. The study does not fit power laws or test their extrapolation.

untested.parts: Only head count/head dimension is varied, at one model size (124.44M) with three settings. Depth-vs-width ratio at fixed parameters, feed-forward ratio and other architecture details are not varied at fixed parameter count. The range is narrow (4× in head count), and no seeds or uncertainty are reported.
No power-law fit of loss against parameters, data or compute. Controlled runs span only about 77M–250M parameters (three points per axis).
No extrapolation from small fits to larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation of parameters versus tokens.
ViT accuracy across sizes is reported, but no power-law form is tested in any modality or regime.
No downstream-task prediction from scale or loss.
No analysis of fitting choices or exponent dependence.

missing.what: Controlled width/depth scaling validation losses for GPT-2-style models: W576 77.40M 3.7021; W768/D12 124.44M 3.5752; W1152 250.36M 3.4000; D9 103.18M 3.6252; D18 166.97M 3.5024. These show loss falling with parameters but over less than one order of magnitude with no fit, so they are context only.
missing.versions: none (context for V1/V4; not a power-law test)

missing.what: LM losses across pretrained families: Qwen2.5 1.5B–14B loss 2.702/2.582/2.457/2.313; BERT Tiny–Large MLM loss 4.594/3.033/3.094/3.102. These are cross-sectional comparisons, not a scaling fit.

record.verdict_notes: The study is mainly about functional redundancy (CFS), not scaling laws. The V4-relevant result is incidental. The authors frame the 0.007 loss spread as a meaningful performance ordering, but by the V4 standard it is a slight change. With no seeds or uncertainty reported, the ordering itself may be within run-to-run noise. Kaplan et al. also varied head count at fixed parameters, so this is close to the original's own manipulation, but at a single small scale.

versions.untested_parts: No power-law fit of held-out language-model loss against parameters, tokens, or compute; no test over several orders of magnitude.
No prediction from small runs evaluated against much larger runs.
No fixed-compute search for loss-minimising parameter and token allocations.
Tests head decomposition at fixed capacity, but not broad ranges of depth, width, or other architecture choices.
No test of whether a power-law form carries over to other modalities or training regimes.
No downstream-task performance prediction from scale or pretraining loss.
No analysis of fitting choices, exponent dependence, or departures from fitted power-law curves.

relationships.condition: Three 12-layer, width-768 GPT-2-style models at identical 124.44M parameters trained under a shared protocol, with head decompositions 6×128, 12×64 and 24×32
relationships.reason: Validation loss ranges only 3.5707–3.5780 (about 0.2%) across a 4× change in head count (r1–r3), so the shape change alters loss only slightly. Single runs with no uncertainty reported.
relationships.display_finding: Validation loss ranged from 3.5707 to 3.5780, about 0.2%, across a fourfold change in attention heads in single runs.
